\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Rolling}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: speed or acceleration, a ring with a block attached on release | steps: energy conservation with rolling ring and block; instantaneous centre of rotation; position of block gives moment of inertia; solve speed | I: block fixed to the ring shifts the instantaneous axis}]
A small block of mass $m$ is rigidly attached at `P' to a ring of mass $m$ and radius $r$. The system is released from rest at $\theta=30^\circ$ and rolls without sliding. The speed of centre of mass of system when block reaches the bottom is
\bfig{84.2}{SI01_p1_phy_s1_q03_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\sqrt{rg}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\sqrt{rg}}{2}$}
\opt{C}{$\sqrt{\dfrac{rg}{2}}$}
\opt{D}{none}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Torque}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: angular velocity, hinge force of a falling square plate hinged at a vertex | steps: moment of inertia about vertex M a^2 2/3; energy conservation as centre of mass falls; torque and hinge reaction at lowest and horizontal positions; check | I: hinge reaction needs both torque and centripetal terms}]
A square plate of mass `M' and edge `a' is hinged at one of its vertex and is allowed to fall down in a vertical plane as shown in figure:
\bfig{88.0}{SI05_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The reaction along the line joining centre \& hinge becomes zero when the plate moves by an angle $\theta=53^\circ$ from vertically upward line.}
\opt{B}{The hinge reaction when the centre comes into the same horizontal line as hinge is $\dfrac{mg}{4}$}
\opt{C}{The max angular acceleration of the plate is $\dfrac{3g}{2\sqrt2a}$}
\opt{D}{The max speed of the COM of the plate is $\sqrt{1.5ag}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Rolling}, answer={A,B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: rolling sphere on rough incline with friction, contact point statements | steps: acceleration g sin theta/(1 + 2/5); friction force; condition mu for rolling without slipping; energy; check options | I: required friction coefficient for pure rolling}]
A solid sphere of mass M and radius R is allowed to roll down a rough inclined plane of angle $\theta$. The centre of the sphere is at a height `h' above the ground.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If $\mu=\dfrac27\tan\theta$, the solid sphere can roll without slipping.}
\opt{B}{If $\mu=\dfrac{\tan\theta}7$, the time taken by sphere to reach the bottom is $\dfrac1{\sin\theta}\sqrt{\dfrac{7h}{3g}}$}
\opt{C}{If $\mu=\dfrac{\tan\theta}7$, the angular speed of the sphere at the bottom is $\sqrt{\dfrac{10g}{7R}}$}
\opt{D}{If $\mu=\dfrac{\tan\theta}7$ the angular acceleration of the sphere is $\dfrac{5g\sin\theta}{14R}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Rolling}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: disc, slipping on a rough surface with initial spin | steps: friction acts till rolling begins; v and omega evolve linearly; final velocity v = (v0 + R omega0 /…)/…; time; check | I: slipping phase ends when v = omega R}]
A disk of mass M and radius `R' is moving on a rough horizontal surface with COM speed $v_0$ and some angular speed. If P is the point of contact of the disk with ground and Q is the highest point then
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{for $\omega_0=\dfrac{v_0}R$ the magnitude of angular momentum about point P would always be $\dfrac32mv_0R$}
\opt{B}{for $\omega_0=\dfrac{v_0}R$ the magnitude of angular momentum about point `P' can be $\dfrac{mv_0R}2$}
\opt{C}{for $\omega_0=\dfrac{v_0}R$ the angular momentum about a point taken on ground at a distance more than `2R' from centre should remain conserved}
\opt{D}{for $\omega_0=\dfrac{v_0}R$ the disk should roll without slipping.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=single, subtopic={Angular momentum}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: angular momentum conservation about the edge for a disc rolling into a ledge | steps: angular momentum about the step edge conserved at impact; I about edge; speed after; minimum speed to climb; evaluate | I: conserve angular momentum about the point of impact}]

In order for it to climb the step, we need $u>u_1$ and for the disc not to bounce, we need $u<u_2$. Taking $g=10$ m/s$^2$ and $\sqrt{15}=3.88$ match the quantities mentioned in List--I with their magnitudes in SI units in List--II.
\bfig{154.5}{SI05_p1_phy_s2_q09_1.png}

(P) & If $u=1$ m/s, the angular velocity of the disc immediately after impact & (1) & 7/27\\ \hline
(Q) & $u_1$ & (2) & 1.41\\ \hline
(R) & $u_2-u_1$ & (3) & 1.50\\ \hline
(S) & If $u=1$ m/s and mass of disc $=$ 1 kg, the horizontal component of the impulse that the disc experiences from the step. & (4) & 10/9\\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P1-PHY-S2-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Rolling}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: cylinder pulled at its centre, mass on a rough surface | steps: friction direction depends on slipping; acceleration and angular acceleration; rolling condition; check | I: friction may act in either direction depending on the parameters}]
A horizontal force $F$ is applied at the center of mass of a cylindrical object of mass $m$ and radius $R$, perpendicular to its axis as shown in the figure. The coefficient of friction between the object and the ground is $\mu$. The center of mass of the object has an acceleration $a$. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$. Given that the object rolls without slipping, which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
\bfig{107.3}{SI09_p1_phy_s2_q05_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{For the same $F$, the value of $a$ does not depend on whether the cylinder is solid or hollow}
\opt{B}{For a solid cylinder, the maximum possible value of $a$ is $2\mu g$}
\opt{C}{The magnitude of the frictional force on the object due to the ground is always $\mu mg$}
\opt{D}{For a thin-walled hollow cylinder, $a=\dfrac{F}{2m}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Angular momentum}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: particle moving under constant force with given start: angular momentum, torque | steps: force constant from initial position; trajectory; angular momentum L = r x p about origin; torque; check | I: torque of constant force about origin as time varies}]
A particle of mass $M=0.2$ kg is initially at rest in the $xy$-plane at a point ($x=-\ell$, $y=-h$), where $\ell=10$ m and $h=1$ m. The particle is accelerated at time $t=0$ with a constant acceleration $a=10\ \text{m/s}^2$ along the positive $x$-direction. Its angular momentum and torque with respect to the origin, in SI units, are represented by $\vec L$ and $\vec\tau$, respectively. $\hat i$, $\hat j$ and $\hat k$ are unit vectors along the positive $x$, $y$ and $z$-directions, respectively. If $\hat k=\hat i\times\hat j$ then which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The particle arrives at the point ($x=\ell$, $y=-h$) at time $t=2$ s.}
\opt{B}{$\vec\tau=2\hat k$ when the particle passes through the point ($x=\ell$, $y=-h$)}
\opt{C}{$\vec L=4\hat k$ when the particle passes through the point ($x=\ell$, $y=-h$)}
\opt{D}{$\vec\tau=\hat k$ when the particle passes through the point ($x=0$, $y=-h$)}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Assume that both the rod and the disc have uniform density and they remain horizontal during the motion. An outside stationary observer finds the rod rotating with an angular velocity $\Omega$ and the disc rotating about its vertical axis with angular velocity $4\Omega$. The total angular momentum of the system about the point O is $\left(\dfrac{Ma^2\Omega}{48}\right)n$. The value of $n$ is \underline{\hspace{2.5em}}.
\bfig{154.6}{SI09_p1_phy_s4_q08_1.png}
\end{bankq}

A block of weight $\alpha W$ is attached at the point $P$ of the beam, as shown in the figure (not to scale). The rope can sustain a maximum tension of $(2\sqrt2)W$. \bfig{146.1}{SI09_p2_phy_s1_q01_1.png}

\opt{A}{The vertical component of reaction force at $O$ does \textbf{not} depend on $\alpha$}

\opt{C}{The tension in the rope is $2W$ for $\alpha=0.5$}
\opt{D}{The rope breaks if $\alpha>1.5$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The expression for the angular momentum of a point mass about origin is given by $\vec{\mathrm L}$ = 2$\alpha$t$\,\ell$n$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm t}{\mathrm t+1}\right)\hat{\mathrm k}$ where $\alpha$ is a certain constant and `t' is time in seconds.

\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA41-P1-PHY-S4-Q05, source={Score Advanced - Test 41}, paper=1, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={Rolling}, answer={2}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: horizontal speed, the axis of a carpet roll unrolling on a floor | steps: energy conservation: the carpet roll radius decreases while the unrolled part lies flat; rolling without slipping v = omega R for the roll; potential energy lost m g (centre of mass drop); kinetic energy includes rotation of the roll and translation | I: unrolling lowers the centre of mass of the remaining roll}]

At the instant shown in the figure rod's angular velocity is $\vec\omega$ and velocity of the centre of mass of the rod is $\vec v_{cm}$. The moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through its centre of mass and parallel to $\hat k$ is $I_{CM}$ and the moment of inertia of the rod about an axis passing through point $A$ and parallel to $\hat k$ is $I_A$. $\vec L_A$ and $K$ represent the angular momentum of the rod about point $A$ and kinetic energy of rod respectively.

\opt{A}{$\vec L_A=I_A\vec\omega=\left(I_{cm}+\dfrac{m\ell^2}{4}\right)\vec\omega,\ K=\dfrac12mv_{cm}^2+\dfrac12I_{cm}\omega^2$}
\opt{B}{$\vec L_A=I_A\vec\omega=m\vec r_{cm}\times\vec v_{cm}\,\vec\omega,\ K=\dfrac12mv_{cm}^2+\dfrac12I_{cm}\omega^2$}
\opt{C}{$\vec L_A=I_A\vec\omega=\left(I_{cm}+\dfrac{m\ell^2}{4}\right)\vec\omega,\ K=\dfrac12I_A\omega^2$}
\opt{D}{$\vec L_A=I_A\vec\omega=m\vec r_{cm}\times\vec v_{cm}+I_{cm}\vec\omega,\ K=\dfrac12I_A\omega^2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{D}{$\dfrac{mgr}{\omega_sI_s}$}
\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=TMAS02-P2-PHY-S3-G3-4, source={TMAS - Test 02 (06 Aug 2023)}, questions={3-4}]
The governing equation $\vec\tau=\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt}$, for rigid body motion bears formal resemblance to the translational equation $\vec F=\dfrac{d\vec P}{dt}$ where linear momentum $\vec P=M\vec v$ always holds true as $M$ does not have only directional value. On the other hand for rotational about fixed axis writing $\vec L=I\vec\omega$ can not be correct as $I$ has orientational value for rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis, angular momentum can still be written as $\vec L=I_{xx}\vec\omega_x+I_{yy}\vec\omega_y+I_{zz}\vec\omega_z$ about three mutually perpendicular axes if there axes are symmetrical with respect to body. Symmetry we mean that with chosen coordinates axes $\sum m_ix_iy_i,\ \sum m_iy_iz_i\ \&\ \sum m_ix_iz_i$ are all zero.\par
Such axes are called principal axes. For a body with cylinderical symmetry, axis of revolution is a principal axis and other two principal axes are mutually perpendicular and lie in a plane through centre of mass, perpendicular to axis of rotation. Kinetic energy in pure rotation can then be written as\par\noindent\hfill{\small$K=\dfrac12I_{xx}\omega_x^2+\dfrac12I_{yy}\omega_y^2+\dfrac12I_{zz}\omega_z^2$}\hfill\null\par

\bfig{68.8}{TMAS02_p2_phy_s3_para3_4_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankq}[id=NUR04-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Nurture (General) - Test 04 (11 Feb 2024)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Torque}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=solved, working={alpha=2g cos(theta)/3R, w\^{}2=4g sin(theta)/3R, a\_cm and N from the tangential and centripetal components}, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: disc swinging about a rim axis, torque | steps: angular acceleration; energy for omega; centre of mass acceleration; axle force}]
Consider a uniform disk of mass M and radius R, which is allowed to rotate about a smooth horizontal axis passing through a point on the rim as shown in figure. When the disc rotates by angle $\theta$ as shown in figure,\par
\bfig{134.8}{NUR04_p1_phy_s2_q08_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}

\opt{C}{Contact force between axle of axis of rotation and disk as a function of angular displacement is given by $N=\dfrac{Mg}3\sqrt{1+48\sin^2\theta}$}

\end{qoptions}
